title: `panic` and `recover`: the two places where they belong

videos.script: Lessons 32 to 35 were about errors, the failures a program expects. This lesson is about the other kind of failure: the bug. {{crash}} A slice read one place past its end. A map that nobody made. Go stops the program, prints what went wrong and where, and exits with status 2. That is a panic. {{defer}} Before the program stops, something still runs. The calls you deferred run on the way out, last in, first out, whether the function returns or panics. That is how a file gets closed on every path out of a function. {{recover}} Then recover, which stops a panic. It only works inside a deferred call, and it belongs in two places. One is a boundary that has to survive one bad request. Go's own web server does it for every request, and you will watch it keep serving. The other is inside a package that panics to climb out of deep code, and hands its caller an ordinary error. {{limits}} Last, what recover cannot catch: a panic in another goroutine, and a fatal error such as a stack overflow. By the end you can tell a bug from an error, and you know where a recover belongs and where it would hide a bug.
